nameStory: The American Wigeon gets its name from an old English word for a type of duck, while its nickname 'baldpate' comes from the striking white or cream-colored crown on the male's head. This white cap makes the drake look like he's wearing a pale skullcap, earning him this distinctive moniker that's been used by hunters and birdwatchers for generations.
description: The American Wigeon is a medium-sized dabbling duck that's a common sight on New England's ponds and marshes. Males sport a distinctive white crown stripe and green patch behind the eye, while females are more subdued in warm brown tones. These ducks are about the size of a small chicken, with a compact build and a relatively short, blue-gray bill that's perfect for their plant-heavy diet.

idTips.label: Male's white crown stripe
idTips.description: Breeding males have a bright white or cream stripe running from the forehead to the back of the head, creating a bold contrast against darker sides

idTips.label: Compact blue-gray bill
idTips.description: The bill is noticeably shorter and stubbier than most other ducks, with a distinctive blue-gray color and black tip

idTips.label: Male's green eye patch
idTips.description: A glossy emerald-green patch sweeps back from each eye on breeding males, shimmering in sunlight

idTips.label: White belly and undertail
idTips.description: Both sexes show bright white on the belly and under the tail, especially visible when the duck tips forward to feed

idTips.label: Whistling call
idTips.description: Males give a distinctive three-note whistle that sounds like 'whee-whee-whoo,' often heard before you see the bird

habitat: Look for American Wigeons on shallow freshwater ponds, marshes, and slow-moving rivers throughout New England, especially areas with abundant aquatic vegetation. They favor spots where they can tip forward to reach underwater plants, often joining flocks of coots and other ducks in marshy areas. During migration, they also visit coastal salt marshes and estuaries.

seasonality.spring: Males arrive in full breeding plumage with brilliant white crowns and green eye patches, often seen in courtship displays on open water.
seasonality.summer: Some pairs remain to nest in northern New England, though most continue north; look for family groups with ducklings in marshy areas.
seasonality.fall: Large flocks gather during migration, with males beginning to show fresh breeding colors mixed with duller eclipse plumage.
seasonality.winter: Present in smaller numbers on ice-free water, often in mixed flocks with other ducks, males in subdued winter plumage.

funFact: American Wigeons are notorious 'thieves' that follow diving ducks like Canvasbacks underwater, then steal the aquatic plants right out of their bills when they surface – earning them the nickname 'poacher' among waterfowl enthusiasts.
confusionNotes: Female wigeons can be confused with female Gadwalls, but wigeons have that distinctive short, blue-gray bill and more contrasting white belly. Remember: 'Wigeon's got the white' – both the male's crown and both sexes' bright white bellies are key distinguishing features.
contextualKnowledge: The American Wigeon was formerly classified in the genus Anas with most other dabbling ducks, but recent genetic studies moved it to the genus Mareca along with other wigeons worldwide. This reclassification better reflects their evolutionary relationships and specialized feeding behaviors.
compareHints: Compared to its closest relative the Gadwall, American Wigeons have much more contrasting plumage with that bright white belly, while Gadwalls are more uniformly gray-brown. The Eurasian Wigeon, a rare visitor to New England, has a cream-colored (not white) forehead and rusty-red head sides instead of green.

relatedSpecies.distinction: Gadwalls are much more subdued than their Mareca cousins - American wigeons show bold white crown stripes and green eye patches, while Eurasian wigeons display rusty-red heads.
Compared to its close relative the American Wigeon, the Eurasian Wigeon male has a rusty-red head with cream forehead stripe versus the American's gray face with white crown stripe.
